The black scraper, Thamnaconus modestus, is a commercially important monacanthid found in the coastal waters of the northwestern Pacific. Maximum reported total length in this species corresponds to an ultimate total length of 37.4 centimeters [Li = 37.4 centimeters], a size that is consistent with the upper range observed among related filefish. At the other end of the life cycle, newly hatched larvae emerge as yolk-sac larvae at a minute size; based on an allometric relationship derived from related species, the wet weight at birth is estimated to be 205.8 grams [Wwp = 205.8 grams], reflecting the considerable provisioning of the relatively large, yolk-laden egg. This substantial initial mass is atypical among teleosts and likely supports a prolonged endotrophic larval phase, giving the larvae a temporal buffer to find suitable feeding conditions before the yolk reserves are exhausted. The corresponding body length at the moment of hatching, while not directly measured, is inferred from congeneric data to be minimal relative to the eventual adult size attained over the course of the species' benthic juvenile and demersal adult stages.

Understanding the onset of reproductive capability in Thamnaconus modestus requires consideration of both body size and age. The total length at puberty is estimated to be 25.9 centimeters [Lp = 25.9 centimeters], a value derived from comparative data on related monacanthids and representing the length at which fifty percent of individuals are expected to exhibit gonadal maturation. This length threshold marks a significant inflection point in the species' life history, after which energy is increasingly directed toward gametogenesis. The associated wet weight at puberty is approximately 0.000097 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000097 grams], a value calculated from the estimated egg diameter of a congeneric species and assuming a spherical egg morphology. This extraordinarily low weight at puberty highlights that the onset of reproductive maturity in this species is tied more closely to attaining a requisite body length than to reaching a substantial absolute somatic mass, a pattern common among pelagic spawning fishes.

At a stable water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is estimated to be 10 years [am = 10 years], a duration that places Thamnaconus modestus among the longer-lived members of the Monacanthidae family. This longevity is likely facilitated by the species' moderate metabolic rate at this temperature and its capacity for iteroparous reproduction across several consecutive spawning seasons. In reproductively active females, the gonadosomatic index (GSI) reaches a value of 15% [GSI = 15%] at a water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This index, representing the proportional contribution of ovarian mass to total body mass, indicates a moderate investment in gamete production per spawning batch relative to total somatic mass, consistent with a strategy of producing multiple, smaller clutches over an extended spawning period rather than a single massive reproductive event.

At the upper boundary of somatic growth, the ultimate wet weight attained by Thamnaconus modestus is estimated at 610.5 grams [Wwi = 610.5 grams], a value derived from the length-weight relationship specific to this species. This asymptotic mass is reached as individuals approach their ultimate total length, after which further somatic growth decelerates markedly. Field surveys and fishery landings data suggest that this maximum size is achieved only by the oldest and most successful individuals, typically those that have avoided predation and fishing pressure for the majority of their potential 10-year lifespan (10 years) [am = 10 years] at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. The relatively modest ultimate mass underscores the species' streamlined, laterally compressed body form, which is an adaptation for maneuvering within structurally complex reef and seagrass habitats. This morphology contrasts sharply with the more deep-bodied, heavier species within the same family that occupy open water niches.

Sexual maturation in Thamnaconus modestus involves a gradual transition from the juvenile phase to the spawning adult stage over several months. The total length of 25.9 centimeters [Lp = 25.9 centimeters] at puberty provides a reliable field-based proxy for the onset of reproductive competence, enabling fishery managers to estimate mature proportions from length-frequency data. The minute mass of the eggs, each roughly 0.57 millimeters in diameter, corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 0.000097 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000097 grams], a value consistent with the pelagic egg type that prioritizes high fecundity over per-offspring investment. The spawning season is protracted, with gravid individuals observed from late spring through early autumn. The gonadosomatic index was 15% [GSI = 15%] at 25 °C [T = 25 °C].
